title: The Foundational Lemma: b mod (b−1) = 1
content: Proves $b \bmod (b-1) = 1$ for $b \geq 3$ using Euclidean division: since $b = (b-1) \cdot 1 + 1$ and $1 < b - 1$ (because $b \geq 3$), the remainder is 1. In Lean, `Nat.mod_eq_sub_mod` reduces $b \bmod (b-1)$ to $(b - (b-1)) \bmod (b-1) = 1 \bmod (b-1)$, and `Nat.mod_eq_of_lt` finishes since $1 < b-1$. This single lemma is the universal principle behind all digit-sum divisibility rules.

title: Factor Modular Reduction
content: Proves that if $d \mid (b-1)$, then $b \bmod d = 1$. Writing $b - 1 = dk$ gives $b = dk + 1$, and since $1 < d$, the remainder is 1. The proof extracts the witness $k$ from the divisibility, shows $k \geq 1$ (otherwise $b - 1 = 0$, contradicting $b \geq 2$), then rewrites via `Nat.add_mul_mod_self_left`. This extends the base lemma from $(b-1)$ to any factor of $(b-1)$.

title: The Universal (b−1) Divisibility Rule
content: Three theorems establishing the core divisibility rule: (1) $n \equiv \mathrm{digitsum}_b(n) \pmod{b-1}$ (congruence form), (2) $(b-1) \mid n \iff (b-1) \mid \mathrm{digitsum}_b(n)$ (divisibility iff), and (3) $n \bmod (b-1) = \mathrm{digitsum}_b(n) \bmod (b-1)$ (remainder form). All three are one-line applications of Mathlib's `Nat.modEq_digits_sum` and `Nat.dvd_iff_dvd_digits_sum`, enabled by `base_mod_pred`. This is the generalization of 'casting out nines' to arbitrary bases.

title: Factor Divisibility Test
content: Generalizes the (b−1) rule to any factor $d$ of $(b-1)$: $d \mid n \iff d \mid \mathrm{digitsum}_b(n)$. This single theorem generates all classical digit-sum divisibility tests as special cases. In base 10, since $3 \mid 9$ and $9 = 10 - 1$, we get the divisibility-by-3 rule. In base 16, since $3 \mid 15$ and $5 \mid 15$, we get both mod-3 and mod-5 tests for hexadecimal.

title: Hexadecimal and Octal Specializations
content: Six concrete instantiations: hexadecimal divisibility by 15, 3, and 5 (since $15 = 16-1$ and $3 \cdot 5 = 15$), plus octal divisibility by 7 ($7 = 8-1$), and remainder forms for both bases. Each is a one-line specialization of the general theorems, with divisibility witnesses provided as `⟨k, by omega⟩`. These demonstrate the practical utility: a programmer can test divisibility by 5 in hex by summing hex digits.
mathContext: Base 16: $15 \mid n \iff 15 \mid \mathrm{hexsum}(n)$; $3 \mid n \iff 3 \mid \mathrm{hexsum}(n)$; $5 \mid n \iff 5 \mid \mathrm{hexsum}(n)$. Base 8: $7 \mid n \iff 7 \mid \mathrm{octsum}(n)$.

title: Computational Verification via native_decide
content: Three concrete examples verified by `native_decide`: $15 \mid 255$ (since $\mathrm{0xFF}$ has hex digit sum 30), $15 \nmid 256$ (since $\mathrm{0x100}$ has hex digit sum 1), and $7 \mid 511$ (since $\mathrm{0o777}$ has octal digit sum 21). These bridge the abstract algebraic proofs to concrete computation, showing the theorems produce correct results on specific inputs.

title: Cross-Base Divisibility Theorem
content: The most surprising result: if $d$ divides both $(b_1 - 1)$ and $(b_2 - 1)$, then $d \mid \mathrm{digitsum}_{b_1}(n) \iff d \mid \mathrm{digitsum}_{b_2}(n)$. The proof is elegant—rewrite both sides through $d \mid n$ using `dvd_factor_iff`. The example shows $3 \mid \mathrm{decimalsum}(n) \iff 3 \mid \mathrm{hexsum}(n)$: divisibility by 3 can be checked equally well in decimal or hexadecimal.

title: Consistency with Parent Proof
content: Two theorems confirming backward compatibility: the general theory reproduces the parent proof's base-10 rules for 3 and 9 as special cases. `consistent_div3` instantiates `dvd_factor_iff` with $b=10, d=3$, and `consistent_div9` instantiates `dvd_base_minus_one_iff` with $b=10$. This validates that the generalization is a true extension, not an independent re-derivation.
mathContext: $3 \mid n \iff 3 \mid \mathrm{digitsum}_{10}(n)$ and $9 \mid n \iff 9 \mid \mathrm{digitsum}_{10}(n)$ (recovered as special cases)
